content:
Early voting opened Monday morning in Webb County, and the race for Texas' 28th Congressional District has come down to a single question: who actually brings the money home?

In a story published Saturday, the Laredo Morning Times put that question to both candidates — incumbent Democrat Henry Cuellar and Republican challenger Tano Tijerina — and got two very different answers.

Cuellar's pitch is his seat at the table. After two decades in Congress, he is the ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee's Homeland Security Subcommittee — a position that would make him chairman, the first border-region representative to hold it, if Democrats retake the House in November. His campaign points to recent federal investments it credits him with helping secure: $25 million for the World Trade Bridge expansion, $2.1 million for a Webb County substance-abuse prevention program, and a proposed $772,700 freight-technology project at Texas A&M International University.

Tijerina's answer: the table is overrated. The Webb County judge argues that local governments and agencies — the Metropolitan Planning Organization, grant writers, economic development staff — do the real work of chasing federal dollars, and that Cuellar takes credit for machinery that runs on its own. He points to two current freshmen already sitting on the Appropriations Committee, Reps. Riley Moore of West Virginia and Jefferson Shreve of Indiana, as proof a newcomer can land the seat. He says he has already spoken with Republican leadership about joining the committee in his freshman year.

Cuellar insists that won't happen. "New members do not just join the Appropriations Committee," he told the Times. "They get sent back to the end of the line." The Times notes there is no rule barring freshmen from the committee — Moore and Shreve prove it — but landing a spot still runs through party leadership and seniority.

What the funding fight leaves out

The dueling claims deserve the scrutiny neither campaign will give them, so here it is:

The FEC complaint is still sitting there. A November 2025 complaint alleges Tijerina used an "exploratory committee" to dodge Texas's resign-to-run law — and he admitted on radio the committee existed "because there's a resign to run clause." Unresolved, and unmentioned in the funding debate.

The party-switch timing still stinks. Tijerina won three elections as a Democrat, then became a Republican in December 2024 — weeks after Webb County voted red for the first time in a century, and weeks after hiring a GOP consulting firm.

The pardon still hangs over Cuellar. President Trump pardoned Cuellar and his wife in December 2025 in their federal bribery and money-laundering case, then turned on him in October for staying a Democrat — calling him "disloyal and ungrateful" and a "LOSER" while endorsing Tijerina as "payback."

National Republicans are hedging. The Congressional Leadership Fund pulled $3 million in reserved TV ads from TX-28 on October 14 and moved the money to TX-15 and TX-34. When your own party's super PAC walks away two weeks before early voting, that says something about their internal polling — which the public never gets to see. There has been no recent public polling in the race; the only independent survey, a Texas Southern University poll from August, had Cuellar up 11.

There's a third name on the ballot. Green Party candidate Marlon Duran is also running in TX-28, a fact that rarely makes the headlines but will be on every voter's ballot.

What happens next

Early voting runs October 19–30 at 14 Webb County sites, and Election Day is November 3. A Cuellar win preserves two decades of seniority and a potential subcommittee chairmanship. A Tijerina win sends a freshman to Washington with the full backing of the president, the House speaker, and the majority leader — and a promise, not a guarantee, of an Appropriations seat.

Voters get to decide which version of "bringing home the bacon" they believe.

Update — October 20, 2026

After this story was published, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce entered the race on October 18, endorsing Rep. Henry Cuellar for reelection in TX-28. Rodney Davis, the Chamber's head of government affairs, praised what he described as Cuellar's support of the business community in Congress and said the organization was "proud to endorse him for reelection." Cuellar's campaign can now point to organized business lining up behind him — even as the sitting Republican president has endorsed his opponent.

Update — October 21, 2026

The debate question is now on the table. On October 18, the Washington Examiner reported that Republican challenger Tano Tijerina has accused Rep. Henry Cuellar of declining multiple invitations to debate ahead of the November 3 election, and posted a video issuing a direct challenge. "Henry, I'm inviting you into debate," Tijerina said in the video, adding, "I know you decline multiple requests, but like you said, debate is good for the people to see both candidates."

The Examiner's account did not include a response from Cuellar's campaign, and as of publication Webb Watch 956 has seen no announced debate date or format in TX-28. Tijerina's claim that Cuellar has declined multiple invitations is the challenger's assertion; Cuellar's campaign has not publicly addressed it in the reporting available.

Sources: Laredo Morning Times, Oct. 18, 2026 (Jose De La Rosa); Texas Tribune; Punchbowl News; AdImpact; Texas Southern University August 2026 poll; Cook Political Report; Webb Watch 956 reporting; U.S. Chamber of Commerce press release, Oct. 18, 2026; Washington Examiner, "Debate disputes take center stage in high-stakes Texas midterm races," Oct. 18, 2026.

Webb Watch 956
excerpt: As early voting opens, Cuellar and Tijerina are fighting over who really delivers federal dollars to Laredo — and Webb Watch fact-checks what both men left out.
title: The Money Fight: Cuellar and Tijerina Clash Over Who Really Delivers Federal Dollars as Early Voting Opens
